(CNN) -- President Obama said Tuesday that the country already is "seeing shovels hit the ground" on the first infrastructure repair project funded through the Transportation Department's share of the $787 billion stimulus bill. Workers mark where repairs are needed on Maryland Route 650. Transportation Secretary Ray LaHood said, "The work begins today in Montgomery County, Maryland, where a work crew is starting on a project to resurface Maryland State Highway 650 -- a very busy road that has not been fully repaired in 17 years." The resurfacing contract is going to a Pennsylvania-based family-owned company, American Infrastructure, LaHood said. He said the project will support 60 jobs. "And that's how we're going to get the country back on its feet," LaHood added. Mark Compton, director of government affairs for American Infrastructure, said his company received $2.1 million in federal funds, by way of the Maryland State Highway Administration. The money will be used to repave and add safety features to a stretch of the highway. Compton said the cash infusion is the "catalyst" to create 60 jobs, including bringing back some laid-off employees. He said he hopes the workers can be retained beyond this six-month project. "We'll continue to bid, so the goal is to get more projects to keep those guys working, so they can roll off that project onto another," Compton said. CNNMoney: Stimulus funds hit the street . Obama and LaHood on Tuesday announced the release of $27 billion in funds from the stimulus package "to help states create a 21st-century infrastructure." The president said it is part of the "largest new investment in America's infrastructure since President Eisenhower built the Interstate Highway System." Obama said another 200 construction projects would be launched over the next few weeks, "fueling growth in an industry that's been hard hit by our economic crisis." Two weeks ago, Obama signed into law his stimulus plan, known as the American Reinvestment and Recovery Act. The president has said the plan will create or save up to 3.5 million jobs over the next two years. Four-hundred thousand of those will be infrastructure jobs that include rebuilding roads, bridges and schools. LaHood has asked the nation's governors to certify projects and provide assurances that funds from the act will be spent for appropriate infrastructure projects. Obama said transportation projects would be stamped with a special emblem so people can see where their tax dollars are going. Obama said the investments in highways would create or save 150,000 jobs by the end of 2010. The number of jobs being created or saved in one year is more than the number of jobs the Big Three automakers have lost in manufacturing over the past three years, Obama said. By investing in roads "that should have been rebuilt long ago," Obama said, "we can save some 14,000 men and women who lose their lives each year due to bad roads and driving conditions." "Poor roads are a public hazard, and we have a responsibility to fix them," he said.  Watch Obama explain how the roads will save lives » . Obama also announced Tuesday that the Treasury Department and Federal Reserve were launching the Consumer and Business Lending Initiative. When fully implemented, Obama said, the initiative "will generate up to a trillion dollars in new lending for the American people, and this will help unlock our frozen credit markets, which is absolutely essential for economic recovery." CNNMoney's Aaron Smith contributed to this report.

The president said the funding is part of the “largest new investment in America’s infrastructure since President Eisenhower built the Interstate Highway System.”

Obama said an additional 200 construction projects would be launched over the next few weeks, “fueling growth in an industry that’s been hard hit by our economic crisis.”

(CNN) — President Obama announced Tuesday that work was already getting underway on the first infrastructure-repair project financed by the Transportation Department’s portion of the $787 billion economic stimulus package.

Crews were identifying areas in need of repair along Maryland Route 650. Transportation Secretary Ray LaHood said the effort was beginning that day in Montgomery County, Maryland, where workers would resurface the heavily traveled state highway, which had not undergone a complete repair in 17 years.

According to LaHood, the contract was awarded to American Infrastructure, a family-owned company based in Pennsylvania. He said the project would sustain 60 jobs, adding that efforts like this would help the nation recover.

American Infrastructure’s director of government affairs, Mark Compton, said the company obtained $2.1 million in federal funding through the Maryland State Highway Administration. The funds would pay for repaving part of the road and installing additional safety improvements.

Compton described the federal money as the driving force behind the creation of 60 jobs, some of which would go to previously laid-off workers. Although the project was expected to last six months, he said he hoped the company could keep those employees afterward by continuing to compete for additional contracts. The objective, he explained, was to secure enough new work for employees to move directly from this job to another.

CNNMoney reported that stimulus funding had begun reaching projects.

On Tuesday, Obama and LaHood also announced that $27 billion from the stimulus legislation was being made available to assist states in developing what they called infrastructure suited to the 21st century. Obama characterized the funding as the biggest new commitment to U.S. infrastructure since President Eisenhower’s construction of the Interstate Highway System.

The president said approximately 200 additional construction projects would begin within the coming weeks, providing a boost to an industry severely affected by the economic crisis.

Two weeks earlier, Obama had signed the stimulus measure, formally called the American Reinvestment and Recovery Act, into law. He said the legislation would create or preserve as many as 3.5 million jobs during the following two years. Of those, 400,000 would involve infrastructure work, including repairs and reconstruction of roads, bridges, and schools.

LaHood asked governors across the country to certify proposed projects and guarantee that money provided under the law would be used for eligible infrastructure purposes. Obama said transportation projects funded by the package would display a distinctive symbol so taxpayers could identify where their money was being spent.

Obama projected that highway investments would create or protect 150,000 jobs by the close of 2010. He noted that the number of jobs created or retained in a single year would exceed the total number of manufacturing positions lost by the Big Three automakers over the previous three years.

The president also argued that repairing roads that had long needed reconstruction could help prevent the deaths of roughly 14,000 people annually from unsafe roads and driving conditions. He called deteriorating roads a threat to public safety and said the government had an obligation to repair them. Obama also discussed how better roads could save lives.

In a separate announcement Tuesday, Obama said the Treasury Department and the Federal Reserve were starting the Consumer and Business Lending Initiative. Once fully operational, he said, the program could produce as much as $1 trillion in new loans for Americans. He added that the initiative would help restart frozen credit markets, a step he described as essential to economic recovery.

CNNMoney’s Aaron Smith contributed to the report.

counterfactuals.output:
# Obama announces first transportation project funded by stimulus

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — President Barack Obama announced Tuesday that work is beginning on the first transportation infrastructure project financed through the $787 billion economic stimulus package, marking an early test of his administration’s plan to create jobs through public works spending.

The project will resurface a section of New Hampshire Avenue, also known as Maryland Route 650, in Montgomery County, Maryland. Federal stimulus money will pay for the roadwork, which the administration says will create or preserve construction jobs while improving a heavily traveled commuter route near Washington.

Speaking at the Department of Transportation, Obama said the project demonstrated that money from the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act was beginning to move into the economy.

“We are putting Americans back to work doing the work that America needs done,” Obama said.

Transportation projects are a major component of the stimulus law, which Obama signed in February amid a deepening recession and rising unemployment. The measure includes tens of billions of dollars for highways, bridges, public transit and rail systems.

Administration officials have promoted such projects as “shovel-ready,” meaning construction can begin quickly. States must meet federal deadlines for committing the money or risk losing it to other projects.

Obama said the government would monitor spending closely and make information about stimulus-funded projects available to the public. Critics, including many congressional Republicans, have questioned whether the package is too costly and whether infrastructure spending can be deployed rapidly enough to provide an immediate economic boost.

The White House has said the broader recovery plan will create or save millions of jobs over two years. Economists have cautioned, however, that the full impact of infrastructure investments may take time to reach workers and local economies.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the resurfacing of Maryland Route 650 as the first Transportation Department project financed through the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, including quotes from Obama, Ray LaHood, and American Infrastructure.
counterfactuals.output:
## Maryland Route 650: first ARRA transportation project

On March 3, 2009—two weeks after the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act was signed—federal officials announced that resurfacing Maryland Route 650, or New Hampshire Avenue, would be the first highway project to receive financing under the act.

The roughly $2.1 million project resurfaced a section of MD 650 in Montgomery County, generally between MD 108 and MD 198. It included pavement repairs, milling, resurfacing, new lane markings and related safety work. Maryland moved quickly because the design and environmental work had already been completed, making the project “shovel ready.” The contract went to American Infrastructure’s Maryland division, and work began in March 2009.

President Barack Obama presented the project as evidence that the recovery program was beginning to operate quickly:

> “Just two weeks after I signed our recovery plan into law, we are seeing shovels hit the ground.”

Transportation Secretary Ray LaHood characterized it as the beginning of a much larger national program:

> “This is the first of many highway projects that will help create jobs and put us on the path to economic recovery.”

American Infrastructure, the contractor, said in its announcement:

> “We’re proud to be a part of the first stimulus-funded transportation project in the nation.”

The Route 650 work was symbolically important even though it was modest in size. It was the first federal highway-funding obligation publicly announced under ARRA, demonstrating how the administration intended to channel stimulus money through projects that states could begin almost immediately. Maryland ultimately received hundreds of millions of dollars in Recovery Act transportation funding, while nationwide the law provided about $48 billion for transportation, including more than $27 billion for highways and bridges.

The project’s employment effect was primarily immediate construction activity and preservation of existing jobs at the contractor and its suppliers, rather than the creation of an entirely new permanent workforce. It also drew early attention to the administration’s promises of competitive bidding, public reporting and federal oversight of stimulus spending.

**Principal contemporary sources:** White House remarks at the Department of Transportation, March 3, 2009; U.S. Department of Transportation/Federal Highway Administration announcement of the first ARRA highway obligation; Maryland State Highway Administration project materials; and American Infrastructure’s project announcement.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a detailed 2009 news story explaining how federal stimulus funds are beginning to support road repairs and construction jobs, using the Montgomery County highway project as the main example.
counterfactuals.output:
**Stimulus Dollars Reach the Pavement as Maryland Road Work Begins**  
*Montgomery County project offers an early test of whether Washington’s recovery plan can quickly preserve construction jobs and repair aging highways*

**SILVER SPRING, Md., April 2009** — The first visible signs of the federal economic stimulus are appearing along a busy highway in Montgomery County, where orange barrels, milling machines and road crews have begun turning money approved in Washington into fresh pavement and construction paychecks.

A resurfacing project on Maryland Route 650, better known as New Hampshire Avenue, is among the state’s early transportation projects financed through the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act. The work involves removing deteriorated pavement, repairing damaged sections of the road, improving markings and laying a new asphalt surface along several miles of the heavily traveled corridor.

The project is modest compared with the bridges, interchanges and new highways planned elsewhere. But state and federal officials say it illustrates the central promise of the $787 billion stimulus law signed by President Barack Obama in February: move money quickly into projects that are ready to begin, address long-deferred infrastructure needs and keep contractors and laborers working during the deepest recession in decades.

“This is what the recovery program is supposed to look like,” a Maryland transportation official said as equipment moved down the roadway. “It is a project that was designed, reviewed and ready to go. Federal funding allowed us to move it forward instead of postponing it.”

### From federal legislation to local asphalt

The recovery act includes about $48 billion for transportation nationwide, with roughly $27.5 billion dedicated to highways and bridges. The money is being distributed to states under existing federal transportation formulas, but with unusually tight deadlines intended to prevent funds from sitting unused.

States must obligate a substantial portion of their highway allocations within months or risk having the money redirected. Federal officials also have required states to track spending and report how many jobs are created or preserved.

Maryland is receiving hundreds of millions of dollars for roads, bridges, transit and other transportation work. State officials assembled a list of “shovel-ready” projects—jobs for which engineering, environmental reviews and other preparations were largely complete—so contracts could be advertised quickly.

The New Hampshire Avenue resurfacing was well suited to those requirements. It did not require years of land acquisition or a major environmental study. The pavement was already showing signs of age, and the state had plans in place to repair it.

Without stimulus support, officials said, the project could have been delayed as falling tax revenue forced Maryland to scale back its regular construction program.

### Jobs now, larger effects later

For workers and contractors, the immediate benefit is employment.

Road resurfacing requires equipment operators, truck drivers, laborers, traffic-control crews, asphalt-plant employees, engineers and inspectors. It also generates orders for stone, petroleum-based asphalt, paint, signs and other materials.

The number of people on the highway at any one time may be limited, particularly because some work is performed at night or in stages. But officials say the project supports a broader chain of employment extending from the paving crew to suppliers and subcontractors.

For contractors, that work is especially valuable this year. Private construction has declined sharply as home building has collapsed and businesses have postponed new offices, stores and industrial facilities. Public projects have become one of the few dependable sources of new contracts.

A paving worker at the Montgomery County site said crews had been watching state budgets closely as the recession worsened.

“When projects get canceled, everybody feels it,” he said. “You lose the hours first, and then you start wondering whether there will be another job after this one. If this money keeps projects moving, it keeps people working.”

The Obama administration argues that infrastructure spending has a multiplier effect: a contractor hires or retains workers, those workers continue buying groceries and paying mortgages, and suppliers maintain production. Economists caution, however, that the full effect will take time to measure and that not every dollar produces an entirely new job. Some stimulus-funded projects may preserve positions that otherwise would have disappeared.

That distinction—between creating a job and saving one—is likely to become a central issue as the government begins publishing employment reports.

### An early but limited sign of recovery

The Montgomery County work also demonstrates both the strengths and limitations of infrastructure spending as economic stimulus.

Resurfacing can begin quickly because it is less complicated than building a new highway. It improves safety, reduces vehicle wear and extends the useful life of a road at a lower cost than complete reconstruction.

But a paving contract alone cannot reverse a national downturn. Even a busy project may directly employ only dozens of people, while hundreds of thousands of construction workers nationwide have lost jobs. Large projects capable of employing more workers often require years of planning and cannot begin immediately.

Transportation planners say the recovery program therefore depends on combining many relatively small projects—paving roads, repairing bridges, upgrading signals and improving drainage—across all 50 states.

Federal officials say thousands of such projects are moving through the approval and contracting process. As warmer weather arrives, drivers are expected to see more stimulus-funded construction zones, often identified by signs stating that the work is being financed through the recovery act.

### Scrutiny over speed and spending

The rapid flow of money has also raised concerns about waste, political influence and weak oversight.

Republicans in Congress and other critics have questioned whether the stimulus is too expensive and whether infrastructure spending will arrive soon enough to affect the recession. Watchdog groups have warned that accelerated contracting could increase the risk of inflated bids, poor workmanship or spending on projects with limited long-term value.

Administration officials say existing federal highway rules still apply. States must use competitive bidding, meet safety and engineering standards, comply with wage requirements and submit detailed spending reports. Recovery funds are intended to supplement, rather than replace, regular state transportation spending.

That last requirement is important. If states simply cut their own highway budgets and substitute federal money, the stimulus would produce less additional construction than Congress intended.

Maryland officials say the projects being financed through the act are priorities that could not otherwise proceed on the same schedule because the state’s transportation revenues have weakened. Gas-tax collections and vehicle-related fees have suffered as residents drive less and delay major purchases.

### A practical benefit for commuters

For motorists on New Hampshire Avenue, the most immediate result will be a smoother trip after weeks of lane closures, construction noise and shifting traffic patterns.

The highway carries commuters, buses, delivery vehicles and local traffic through one of the Washington region’s most congested suburban areas. Years of heavy use, winter freezing and repeated patching have left portions of the pavement cracked and uneven.

Crews will mill away the worn surface, make deeper repairs where needed and apply new layers of asphalt. Fresh lane markings and related safety work will follow. Transportation officials say resurfacing now should prevent water from penetrating the roadway and causing more expensive structural damage later.

Work is being scheduled to reduce disruption, though officials warn that drivers should expect delays and allow extra travel time.

### A test case for the recovery act

The Montgomery County project will not settle the national debate over the stimulus. Its economic effects are too small and too local for that. But it provides an early, concrete example of how the administration’s plan is beginning to operate.

Only weeks ago, the money existed as a line in a massive federal law. It then moved through the U.S. Department of Transportation to the state, into a construction contract and finally onto the road in the form of wages, diesel fuel, aggregate and hot asphalt.

For Washington policymakers, the orange barrels are evidence that the recovery effort is advancing from legislation to construction. For Maryland transportation officials, the money means a needed repair can be completed sooner. And for the men and women working beside the highway, the stimulus is measured less in billions of dollars than in hours on the job.

Whether thousands of projects like this one can produce a broader economic recovery remains uncertain. But in Montgomery County, at least, federal stimulus money has begun to reach the pavement.

# Obama Releases $27 Billion for Transportation Projects, Unveils Broader Lending Push

**WASHINGTON —** President Barack Obama’s administration is releasing $27 billion for highway and bridge projects as part of its effort to revive the economy, modernize aging infrastructure and put Americans back to work.

The transportation funding comes from the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, the $787 billion economic stimulus package enacted in February 2009. State and local governments will use the money to repair roads and bridges, reduce congestion and advance projects that can begin quickly.

The administration estimates that the investment will create or preserve roughly 150,000 jobs by the end of 2010. Those positions are expected to include construction workers, engineers and equipment operators, as well as jobs at companies supplying concrete, steel, asphalt and other materials.

Officials have stressed that the money should move rapidly into the economy. States face deadlines for committing the funds, while federal agencies are expected to monitor projects and disclose spending to the public. The emphasis on “shovel-ready” construction reflects the administration’s goal of producing near-term employment while making improvements that support long-term commerce.

The jobs figure is an administration estimate and includes both positions created directly by construction and employment supported indirectly through suppliers and increased consumer spending.

The infrastructure announcement is one part of a broader strategy to address the recession. The administration is also launching a **Consumer and Business Lending Initiative** aimed at restarting credit markets that had largely frozen during the financial crisis.

The initiative builds on the Federal Reserve’s Term Asset-Backed Securities Loan Facility, or TALF. By combining Federal Reserve financing with government capital, officials said the program could support as much as $1 trillion in new lending.

Its initial focus includes loans that affect households and smaller companies, such as auto loans, credit-card lending, student loans and Small Business Administration-backed credit. The administration also plans to broaden the effort to other markets, including certain commercial real-estate loans.

The lending initiative is intended to address a central weakness in the economy: even viable consumers and businesses have struggled to obtain financing as banks tighten standards and investors retreat from markets that traditionally fund loans. By encouraging investors to purchase securities backed by consumer and business debt, the government hopes to lower borrowing costs and increase the availability of credit.

Together, the transportation investment and lending initiative reflect the administration’s two-track response to the downturn. Infrastructure spending is designed to generate immediate demand and employment, while the credit program seeks to restore the flow of private financing needed for a sustained recovery.

Administration officials acknowledge that neither effort will produce results overnight. Transportation projects must move through state contracting systems, and lenders will participate in the credit program only if economic conditions and government terms make doing so attractive. Nevertheless, the White House argues that putting construction money to work and repairing lending markets are both essential to stabilizing the economy.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

**CNN REPORT — STIMULUS MONEY “HITS THE STREET”**

**ANCHOR:**  
Federal stimulus dollars are beginning to translate into visible construction work. In Maryland, crews are repairing a section of Route 650 in what the Obama administration describes as an early sign that its economic recovery plan is taking effect.

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
The Route 650 project is expected to create or restore about 60 jobs, providing work for construction crews while improving the heavily traveled roadway.

Maryland officials say this is only the beginning. The state plans to move ahead with approximately 200 additional construction projects supported by federal recovery funds. The administration argues that projects like these can quickly put money into local economies through wages, contracts and purchases of materials.

President Barack Obama has pointed to the roadwork as evidence that stimulus money is “hitting the street.” He says the broader recovery program will save or create jobs, modernize infrastructure and help pull the country out of the recession.

But the administration’s claims remain subject to scrutiny. Many projects will take time to begin, and economists caution that it may be difficult to distinguish jobs directly created by the stimulus from those that might otherwise have existed.

For Maryland workers on Route 650, however, the impact is immediate: active construction, paychecks and the prospect of hundreds more projects getting underway.

**ANCHOR:**  
The White House says the pace of spending will accelerate as states approve contracts and begin additional transportation and infrastructure work.
